fe8588c782:
This chapter is about getting machine-readable output out of a model that only produces text. It also covers what to do when that output is malformed, inconsistent or wrong.

We follow the output from start to finish. It begins with the request, where a tool’s input schema is the contract. Then come the guarantees the API gives you, and the ones it can’t. After that, the validation layers you own: JSON Schema, Pydantic, business rules, grounding checks. Then the retry loop that feeds specific errors back, and the cases where no retry can help because the answer isn’t in the document.

The chapter ends with the analytics fields (detected_pattern) that make false positives measurable. Implementations are in Python and Java/Spring.
4d60e7bb17:
Declare the output as a tool whose input_schema is your contract, and let the API hand you a parsed object instead of text you have to parse: this removes JSON syntax errors and nothing else.

Everything the schema cannot express (a total that does not match its line items, a PO number that was never printed, a date in the wrong century) is a semantic error, and you handle it with your own validation, a bounded retry loop that feeds the specific error back, and an early exit to a human when the information is simply not in the source.
1b9456e5b0:
Task statement 4.3 is the first sentence, and 4.4 is the second. Together they work like the two halves of an input boundary in any enterprise service.

At the edge, you want a contract that rejects malformed payloads before your code sees them. That’s the schema’s job. Behind the edge, you want business validation that rejects well-formed nonsense. That’s what your validators do. And you want a policy for failures: which ones deserve another attempt, which go to a queue, and which should never be retried.

Have you designed a REST ingestion API with Bean Validation on the DTOs, a rules layer behind it, and a dead-letter topic for poison messages? Then you already know the shape of this chapter.

The unusual part is the producer. The upstream system is a probabilistic model. So “valid but wrong” isn’t an occasional defect. It’s the normal residual error. And a retry can improve a result, or make it worse.
998feef9d2:
The official wording for 4.3 lists these knowledge points, and each one gets its own section here:

  • tool use with JSON schemas is the most reliable approach for schema-compliant output;
  • the difference between tool_choice "auto", "any" and forced tool selection;
  • strict schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones;
  • required versus optional versus nullable fields;
  • enums with "other" plus a detail string, and "unclear" values;
  • format normalisation rules alongside the schema.

The wording for 4.4 adds:

  • retry-with-error-feedback (original document, failed extraction, specific validation error);
  • retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source;
  • the limits of retries more generally;
  • self-correction fields such as calculated_total next to stated_total, and a conflict_detected boolean;
  • a detected_pattern field that lets you analyse which constructs trigger false positives.

The home scenario is Structured Data Extraction. But the same machinery shows up in the code-review scenario (findings as typed objects) and in the support scenario (structured handoff summaries).
5bec44f750: Getting structured data out of a language model is older than tool use. Each generation of technique fixed one failure and exposed the next. The exam’s emphasis is the end state of that sequence: schema compliance doesn’t imply correctness, and retries are bounded.
44bd6f01ea:
The idea that two systems should agree on a machine-checkable description of the data between them is much older than AI.

EDI standards in telecom and retail (X12, EDIFACT) fixed field positions and codes decades ago. XML Schema (XSD) gave SOAP services a formal contract in the early 2000s. JSON Schema later played the same role for REST. Java developers know the in-process version: Bean Validation (@NotNull, @Pattern, @Size) on DTOs.

In every one of these, the contract answers “is this message well-formed and in range?” It has never answered “is this message true?” An XSD-valid invoice can have the wrong total.

That distinction is the spine of 4.3 and 4.4. Keep your own experience with it in view. Nobody on a billing platform treated schema validation as correctness validation.
4f4d8e5201:
Early language-model integrations asked for structure in the prompt: “Respond with JSON only, using these keys.” It worked often enough to demo, and failed often enough to hurt in production.

The model generates text one token at a time. Nothing in that process knows about braces. Replies arrived wrapped in a markdown fence, or prefixed by “Here is the JSON”. Some were truncated at the token limit. Some had a trailing comma, or an unescaped quote inside a string value.

Teams wrote regexes to strip fences and repair commas. Then they wrote tests for the regexes. Then they found the failures they couldn’t repair. Section 03 reproduces all of these.
da8dd10aeb:
Providers responded in layers. Some added a “JSON mode” that guaranteed the reply was parseable JSON, but said nothing about its keys. Another trick was to prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace, so the model could only continue a JSON object.

The more durable change was function calling. The request declares functions with a JSON Schema for their parameters. The response returns a typed call, separate from prose.

Libraries soon wrapped the pattern for developers. You define a Pydantic class and generate the schema from it. You force the model to call a function with that schema. You validate the result, and on failure you re-ask with the validation error.

That last step, “validate, then re-ask with the error”, is the retry-with-feedback loop that 4.4 describes. It was standard practice in the open-source ecosystem well before it appeared in an exam guide.
af4579cc1d:
Anthropic’s Messages API generalised the same idea as tool use. Tools are declared with a name, a description and an input_schema. The model answers with a tool_use content block whose input is already a parsed object. And tool_choice lets you constrain whether a tool is called, and which one.

Chapter 01 covered the loop that executes tools. The trick in this chapter is that, for extraction, you don’t execute anything. The “tool” is a shape. Claude fills the shape, you read the arguments, and the tool never runs. The exam guide calls this the most reliable approach for schema-compliant output.
c8c79faed3:
The next step moved the guarantee. It went from “the model usually follows the schema” to “decoding is constrained so it cannot leave the schema”.

The Claude docs call this structured outputs and describe two features. JSON outputs put a schema on the response format. Strict tool use puts strict: true on a tool definition. Both compile the schema into a grammar that limits what the model may emit.

At the time of writing, the page says the response-format parameter is output_config.format. It says an earlier output_format parameter and a beta header have been deprecated, and it lists the supported models and schema keywords. Treat every one of those details as check the docs. This area has changed names within a single year.

For the exam, hold on to the stable idea. Schema-constrained generation eliminates syntax and shape errors. It doesn’t touch meaning.
7fabe43638:
Start from what the model physically does. It emits tokens.

A JSON document is a string with rules about quoting, escaping, commas and nesting. The model has learned those rules statistically from a great deal of JSON, which is why it’s usually right. “Usually” is the problem.

Take a pipeline that processes 50,000 invoices a month and fails on 1 in 200 replies. That’s 250 failures someone has to find, classify and fix. And the failures don’t spread evenly. They cluster on long documents, on unusual characters, and on exactly the cases where a human would also struggle.
c7853b8091: Companion example 01_free_text_json_breaks.py scripts five replies a model can legitimately produce when asked for “JSON only”. It runs a naive json.loads and a defensive parser on each:
afe3ef7813:
The defensive parser is a regex that finds the outermost braces and removes trailing commas. It rescues three of the four recoverable cases, and it can’t rescue the fifth.

The fifth is the dangerous one: an unescaped quote inside a vendor name. No regex repairs that safely, because the repair requires understanding what the author meant.

The defensive parser also has its own failure mode, which this example doesn’t show. It accepts replies that are well-formed but not what you asked for: a single object when you wanted a list, or a field renamed because the model paraphrased your key.

So you pay twice. You maintain a growing parser, and you still need validation behind it.
7ca9e69c9c:
There’s a subtler cost too. If the model must produce both the explanation and the JSON, the two compete for the same output budget and the same stop conditions.

A reply cut off by max_tokens in the middle of a JSON document isn’t parseable at all. Nothing in the text tells you it was truncated unless you look at stop_reason. Free text leaves all of this to you.
1931135a76:
Watch for options like “add a regex to strip markdown fences” or “ask the model, more emphatically, to output JSON only”. Each is a plausible engineering reflex, and the weaker answer. The exam’s preferred mechanism for schema-compliant output is tool use with a JSON schema.

And parsing isn’t the free-text approach’s only weakness. The deeper one is that nothing ever told the model the required shape in a form the API can enforce or check.
a72bc49d3c:
The mechanism has three parts, and you should be able to draw them from memory.

  1. You declare a tool. The declaration is a name, a description, and an input_schema: a JSON Schema describing an object.
  2. You send the document and, usually, a tool_choice that makes the model call that tool.
  3. The response comes back with stop_reason: "tool_use" and a content block of type tool_use. Its input is a JSON object the API has already parsed.

In Python you read block.input, and you have a dict.
504bce4142:
Why is this more reliable than free text? The reason is architectural, not magical.

The model has been trained to emit tool calls in a form the API can parse deterministically. The response structure separates the call from any prose. You’re no longer asking a text generator to double as a serializer.

The syntax problems in section 03 (fences, preambles, trailing commas) can’t occur in block.input, because the API parsed it, not you. The shape problems (missing keys, wrong types) become much rarer, because the schema is part of the request. With strict mode (section 06), they can be excluded by construction.
b913050bdc:
Here’s a point that confuses people with an agent background: an extraction tool is never executed.

In chapter 01, the loop ran a tool and returned a tool_result. Here the tool just carries a schema. You read the arguments, validate them, store them, and finish.

If you do continue the conversation (for a retry, section 13), you still have to pair the tool_use with a tool_result. The pairing rule from chapter 01 doesn’t care that the tool was fictional.
7d0e47e3ca:
Read the schema as a design document. Every line is a decision that later sections justify.

Almost every field is required but nullable ("type": ["string", "null"]). The model must make an explicit statement about every field, and “not in the document” has a legal spelling. The one non-nullable field is vendor_name, since an invoice with no vendor isn’t an invoice.

The service category is an enum with "other" and "unclear", plus a separate detail string. The total appears as stated_total, copied from the page. The line items sit beside it, so your code can compare them.

Dates and currencies carry patterns. The descriptions state the formats and the “never infer” rule. Sections 08 to 11 take these in turn.
5a9954b4fb: The companion example 02_tool_use_round_trip.py runs this call against the fake client. It prints the pieces you should recognise on a real response:
13298ba4ff:
The tool’s name and description are part of the prompt. The model reads them.

A tool named extract with the description “extracts data” gives no guidance about nulls, formats or ambiguity. The description in the definition above states the two rules that prevent most fabrication: null for what isn’t printed, and never infer.

Chapter 05 treats descriptions as the main way agents select tools. The same discipline applies here, with one difference. In extraction there’s one tool, and the description steers values, not selection.

If you use several extraction tools at once (an invoice schema, a credit-note schema, a purchase-order schema), the descriptions are again how the model picks. Section 05 shows the tool_choice setting built for that case.
deaa3028ba:
tool_choice tells the API how much freedom the model has. The exam asks you to tell three behaviours apart, and the docs name a fourth.

They matter for extraction because the failure you’re guarding against isn’t malformed JSON. It’s no tool call at all. With tools declared and nothing else said, the model may decide a short prose answer is enough.
a3ba728cfc: Companion example 03_tool_choice_modes.py scripts a chatty model and runs it against each setting. The fake client enforces the same contract as the real API. With any or tool, a prose-only reply is impossible. So the example rejects the script as something the API would never return:
1862c10ee2:
The docs explain the mechanism. With any or tool, the API prefills the assistant message so that the response begins with a tool call.

The docs spell out one consequence. The model emits no natural-language preamble before the tool_use block, even if you ask for one. If you want an explanation plus a structured call, use auto and put the instruction in the user message (“use the record tool in your response”).

Changing tool_choice between requests also invalidates cached message blocks. That matters if you cache a long document prefix and then vary the setting between a first pass and a retry. Chapter 13 returns to caching and batches.
c842ec956e:
When this chapter was written, the tool-definition page of the docs said forced tool use isn’t supported everywhere.

With manual extended thinking (thinking: {"type": "enabled"}), any and tool return an error. Only auto and none work.

The page also listed specific models (at that time Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, among others) for which any and tool return a 400 regardless of thinking. For those, it recommended auto with strict tool use to guarantee schema-valid inputs, or the JSON-outputs feature for a fixed response shape.

Check the docs for your model before you write forced choice into a design.
cf2a5555fd:
So how does that square with an exam that tests forced selection? The exam tests the concept: what auto, any and forced mean, and which one guarantees a structured call. Answer those questions as written.

In your own systems, there are two ways to get a guaranteed structured call. Use forced choice where the model supports it. Where it doesn’t, use auto plus strict schemas plus a harness-level rule that “no tool call is a failure”.

Companion example 18_forced_choice_rejected_models.py wraps the fake client so the documented model ids raise the documented 400. Then it runs the fallback:
6fe4ef489a:
The fallback has three parts, and the third is easy to forget.

  1. The tool is marked strict.
  2. The system prompt says to answer by calling the tool, not in prose.
  3. The harness treats a response with no tool_use block as a failed attempt. It appends the assistant turn, adds a user message telling the model to call the tool, and counts the attempt against the retry budget.

Skip the third part, and a single prose reply crashes the pipeline with StopIteration on the line that looks for the block.
0adbd3e3e6:
On its own, tool use is highly reliable but not a formal guarantee. The model is trained to follow the schema, yet rare cases still violate it: a number returned as the string "two", or a required key missing.

The Claude docs describe a stronger mechanism, structured outputs, in two forms.

  • Strict tool use sets strict: true on a tool definition. It constrains sampling so the tool name and input match the schema.
  • JSON outputs put a schema on the response format (output_config.format with type: "json_schema" when this chapter was written). They constrain the final text to it.

You can combine them in one request. Both work by compiling the schema into a grammar. The docs say the first use of a schema carries extra latency while the grammar compiles, and that compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use.

Parameter names, supported models, supported schema keywords and the cache behaviour are the details most likely to have moved. Check the docs.
70b8c8c56f:
Strict mode removes the shape errors from section 07’s first two layers: invalid JSON, missing required keys, wrong types, values outside an enum, and extra properties where additionalProperties is false.

If your downstream code deserialises into a typed object, a strict schema makes deserialisation failure essentially impossible. That’s a real operational gain. It’s also why the exam guide’s wording is careful: schema-compliant output with no JSON syntax errors.
43f3dc0349: Meaning. A typed stated_total: 3912.45 copied from the wrong line of the page is perfectly schema-compliant. So is a fabricated PO number in a non-nullable string field. So is "mpls", chosen from a closed enum for a service that isn’t MPLS.
a9ed23560e: Constraints the grammar cannot express. The docs say the SDK helpers strip constraints such as minimum, maximum, minLength and maxLength from schemas sent for strict use. They move them into descriptions and validate the original constraints on the client. Whether patterns and other keywords work in strict mode is something to confirm on the current page. The practical rule: keep your own validator in the pipeline, with the full set of constraints, whether or not you use strict mode.
21c17866c8: Complexity limits. The docs list limits for schemas used with strict tools or JSON outputs. The page we read listed 20 strict tools per request, 24 optional parameters in total, and 16 parameters using anyOf or type arrays. Schemas too complex to compile get an error. A schema where nearly every field is “required but nullable” leans heavily on type arrays, so count them. Check the docs for the current numbers.
90425e5836: Refusals and truncation. The docs say that with structured outputs, a stop_reason of "refusal" returns a 200 and a message that may not match the schema. A "max_tokens" stop can leave incomplete output that doesn’t match it either. Always check stop_reason before you trust the shape, strict or not.
4638189dd0: Incompatibilities. The page lists some. Citations can’t be combined with output_config.format, and message prefilling is incompatible with JSON outputs. If your extraction needs source citations, plan for a quote field in the schema instead of the citations feature (chapter 16 covers provenance).
baee79c285:
The statement “strict schemas guarantee correct values” is false. Exam options built on it are tempting, because strict mode sounds like a complete solution.

The correct reading has two sides. Syntax errors: yes. Semantic errors: no. When an option says a strict schema makes validation, retry or review unnecessary, eliminate it.
0429056bd5:
Three terms get mixed up in discussions of structured output, and the exam’s distractors depend on that confusion.

  • A syntax error means the text isn’t valid JSON at all.
  • A schema error means it’s valid JSON in the wrong shape: a missing key, a string where a number belongs, a value outside the enum.
  • A semantic error means it’s valid JSON in the right shape, with values that are wrong given the source or given each other.

Tool use removes the first. Strict mode removes most of the second. Nothing in the API removes the third, because the API has no access to ground truth. It doesn’t know what the invoice said. It only knows what the model emitted.
c15c9b75c3:
Companion example 04_syntax_vs_semantic.py extracts an MPLS invoice whose last line is a Federal USF surcharge of 162.45.

On the first attempt, the simulated model drops the surcharge. Real models do this sort of thing on documents where a small line sits apart from the table. The result is a record that passes every structural check:
73d7ae0be0:
Everything a schema can see is fine. Only a rule that knows how two fields relate (the lines must add up to the total) notices.

This is the pattern for every semantic check you’ll write. Find a relationship in the domain that must hold if the extraction is right, and test it in code. The table lists typical ones for carrier invoices and for the exam’s other scenarios.
eb104aa30a: Notice the last row. Grounding is the most general semantic check for extraction, and it’s cheap. If a value is meant to be copied from the document, check that it occurs in the document. Section 14 uses it to catch exactly the failure that retries create.
ee78738bc8:
A field can be in one of four states with respect to a schema, and designers regularly conflate them.

The JSON Schema keyword required controls whether the key must be present. The type controls which values are allowed, and ["string", "null"] allows an explicit null. So “required” and “nullable” are independent. The four combinations behave differently when the source document lacks the information.
6e64682e36:
The exam’s wording is “optional or nullable fields for information that may be absent”. Either of the two honest designs satisfies it. The design to avoid is the first row.

Say the schema makes po_number a required, non-null string, and the invoice has no PO number. The model now has to choose: violate the schema, or invent a plausible-looking value. Models usually prefer to satisfy the schema. The invented value then travels downstream looking exactly like a real one.
16006ce4b7: Companion example 05_required_vs_nullable.py runs the invoice with no PO number against both schemas. The simulated model implements the hypothesis. How a real model behaves is an empirical question, and you should measure it on your own documents, as chapter 11 does for prompts:
feb37691d1:
Which of the two honest designs should you choose? For extraction I prefer required and nullable, for a reason that comes from operations.

With an optional field, you can’t tell “the document has no PO” from “the model forgot to look”. With required-and-nullable, every field is an explicit answer, and the model has to consider each one.

A downstream count of nulls per field also becomes a useful quality metric. Suppose po_number is null on 2% of invoices from one carrier and 40% from another. You’ve learned something about the carrier, or about your prompt.

The cost is that nullable fields count towards the complexity limits for strict schemas (section 06), and every extra nullable adds tokens. Where the schema is large, make the genuinely sparse fields optional, and keep the important ones required-nullable.
bd3d8aa92e:
One practical hazard sits in the validators, not the schema.

In Pydantic, a field declared as Optional[str] = None has a default. So a record that omits the key entirely validates cleanly. The JSON Schema you send to the API says the key is required. The Pydantic model you validate with says it isn’t.

Companion example 09_jsonschema_vs_pydantic.py shows the divergence on a record with currency missing. JSON Schema reports one issue. Pydantic reports none.

If a required key matters, either validate with both, or declare the field without a default. In Pydantic v2, currency: Optional[str] with no = None makes the key required but nullable. Section 12 takes the validators in turn.
1080f54b01:
The schema defines what’s allowed. The description tells the model what to do.

For nullable fields, write both halves of the rule: the format of a value when present, and the condition for null. “PO number, as printed. null if no PO is printed. Never infer.” beats “PO number”, because it names the failure you’re trying to prevent: inferring.

Add a free-text notes field too, and tell the model to explain each null or ambiguity there. It costs a few tokens and turns silent nulls into reviewable ones. A human looking at a flagged record sees “No PO number printed; reference line says ‘see contract’”, not just a null.

Chapter 11 covers the few-shot side of the same problem. Its examples include a document with a missing field and the correct null output. That way the model sees the honest behaviour demonstrated, not only described.
8f1629d34c:
An enum turns a free-text category into a closed set your downstream code can switch on. That’s why you want one. The same property is the hazard.

A closed enum asserts that every possible document falls into one of the listed categories. Then a document arrives that doesn’t fit: a Managed SD-WAN invoice, against an enum of ethernet, MPLS, dark fiber, voice trunk and colocation. The model is forced to choose the nearest wrong value.

The output is schema-valid, so nobody notices. Not until a report shows a suspicious volume of “MPLS”.
4a7e7437f1: "other" plus a detail string. The document clearly states a category, but it isn’t one of the values you listed. The detail field carries what the document actually says (“Managed SD-WAN”). This is a signal about your enum. When “other” piles up a cluster with the same detail, add a value.
c032803654: "unclear". The document doesn’t settle the question. It might be a bundle, a scan with the service line cut off, or an invoice that lists charges without naming a service. This is a signal about the document. The right downstream action is human review, or a request for a better source.
30c901695f:
Keep the two apart, because they’re handled differently. “Other” is a data-quality item for the schema owner. “Unclear” is a case-level item for an operator.

Merge them into one “other” value, and you can no longer tell “our taxonomy is incomplete” from “this scan is unreadable”. Companion example 06_enum_other_unclear.py shows both the enum behaviour and the validator that enforces the detail field:
dc4c70e08d:
The last two lines are the half of the design that JSON Schema can’t easily express.

“If category is other then detail must be a non-empty string” is a conditional requirement. JSON Schema can state it with if/then. But strict-mode support for such keywords is something to confirm in the docs. A one-line model validator in Pydantic is simpler, and works regardless.

This is the general division of labour. The schema carries what it can carry portably. Code carries the conditional rules.
9b04954a43:
One more property of the design deserves a mention: enum values are an interface.

Adding a value is cheap if downstream code has a default branch. Removing or renaming one is a breaking change, exactly like an enum in a Java API. So version your tool schema the way you version a DTO.

Keep the enum list in one place that generates both the schema and the Java enum or Python Literal, so they can’t drift. And for the casing caveat from section 06, define values in one canonical case and compare case-insensitively on the way in.
b31eecb174:
Real documents disagree about formats. A date shows up as “03 Aug 2026”, “8/3/26” or “2026-08-03”. An amount shows up as “$1,200.00”, “1.200,00 EUR” or “USD 1200”. A phone number carries spaces, dots, a leading “+1”, or none.

Leave normalisation to downstream code, and every consumer implements its own rules and disagrees with the others. The exam’s wording is to include format normalisation rules in the prompt alongside the schema, so the model emits one canonical format.

Three layers do the work, and each does a different job.
1df0f0cc10: State the target format in the field description and the system prompt. “YYYY-MM-DD.” “Amounts as numbers with no currency symbol or thousands separator; credits negative.” “Currency as ISO 4217 code.” Few-shot examples with varied source formats and one canonical output (chapter 11, section 16) reinforce this more strongly than a description alone.
8e49e4f8dd: Normalise in code what you can parse unambiguously, and refuse to guess the rest. “03 Aug 2026” has exactly one reading. “8/3/26” has two: August 3 or March 8. Repairing the first in code is free and saves a retry. Guessing the second is how silent errors start. Send it back to the model with a specific question, or to a human.
bb1818a7c6:
The row to notice is “(450.00)”. Accountants write negatives in parentheses. A normaliser that simply strips every non-digit character turns a credit of (450.00) into a charge of 450.00.

No schema will catch that semantic error. So the example handles it explicitly (parentheses mean negative), and the tests in section 18 should pin the rule.

Normalisation rules need tests built from your actual documents. The formats above are just the ones that happened to be in this corpus.
bcd3c25556:
You can, for formats you control. The model’s advantage is that it understands context code can’t see. Which of three dates on the page is the invoice date? Is “12/05” a month and day, or a month and year, given the surrounding text?

The division that works: the model decides which value and emits it in a canonical format. Code validates the format and normalises the unambiguous leftovers.

Chapter 16 discusses what to do when even the model is unsure. Have it say so, with a confidence signal you calibrate, instead of guessing.
ed4b9b7ef6:
Section 07 introduced the check that line items must add up to the total. A better design asks the model to expose the numbers it used, so the disagreement is visible in the record itself.

The pattern in the exam guide is to extract three things:

  • stated_total, the figure printed on the document;
  • calculated_total, the model’s own sum of the line items;
  • a conflict_detected boolean that is true when they differ.

Add a short conflict_detail string for what disagrees.
f2ef91b544:
Why not simply tell the model, “make sure the total is right”? Because that instruction sets a goal it can meet the wrong way.

A model asked to reconcile can change a line amount to make the sum match. Or it can replace the printed total with its own sum. Either way you get a record that’s internally consistent and doesn’t match the document.

The self-correction fields flip the incentive. The model is asked to report a disagreement, not hide it. A conflict in the output is information, and the record is more useful for having it.
9f44a16fdb: Companion example 10_self_correction_fields.py runs three invoices. The simulated model fills the three fields from what it extracted. Alongside, the harness computes its own sum with Decimal:
72cbd27c1a:
Two cases, two different causes, one signal.

In missed_surcharge, a line item was dropped. The retry should say “re-check for missed lines”. In prev_balance, the stated total came from the wrong figure: the previous balance of 10,114.00 sits next to the real amount due of 3,200.00. Here the retry should say “this looks like a different figure”.

The record tells you the numbers. conflict_detail lets the model explain, and your feedback message (section 13) can use that.
8f22de5ef6:
The self-correction fields are evidence, not proof. Language models make arithmetic mistakes. A model that miscalculates its own calculated_total can report conflict_detected: false with confidence.

So the harness recomputes the sum in code, from the extracted line items. It compares both its own sum and the model’s calculated_total with the stated total. Two checks follow:

  • (1) Your sum must match the stated total. If it doesn’t, the record fails, whatever the model claimed.
  • (2) Your sum should equal the model’s calculated_total. A mismatch there means the model can’t add. That’s a separate quality signal, and worth logging.
4830b79625:
On the Java side of this check, your instincts help. Never accumulate currency in double. Binary floating point can’t represent 0.1 exactly, and the error compounds over line items. The companion Java program prints 0.30000000000000004 for 0.1 + 0.2.

Parse the amounts as BigDecimal from the JSON text, and sum with add. Compare with a cent-sized tolerance that you chose on purpose. Some carriers round per line, so the total can differ by a cent.
574777b3d6:
The first message in the file’s output is the one a retry will carry: line items sum to 3750.00 but stated_total is 3912.45. The second branch, a null stated total, is the one that must not trigger a retry. Section 14 explains why.

With Jackson, keep amounts exact by configuring the ObjectMapper with DeserializationFeature.USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS. Then a JSON number such as 3912.45 never passes through a double (check the Jackson docs for your version).
1a42cb9c86:
Validation is a stack, and each layer is cheap compared with the one above it.

Run them in order, and stop at the first layer that reports problems. Later layers assume a well-shaped record: a semantic check that sums line_items will crash on a record with no line_items.

Every layer returns the same type, a list of issues. Each issue carries the field path, a code for the kind of problem, and a message written for the model to read. That uniform type is what lets one retry loop serve all layers.
97dceddf03:
The schema you send to the API is also a validator. Running it on your side costs nothing. It catches the cases strict mode doesn’t: keywords the grammar can’t enforce, models or modes where strict is off, and records that came from somewhere other than a live API call, such as a cache or a message queue.

Use Draft202012Validator, iterate over iter_errors, and keep the path.
0434e30bce: Companion example 09_jsonschema_vs_pydantic.py sends six malformed records through both validators. Memorise the summary of what it shows. It tells you why to run both:
68e7c6aaeb:
You can also generate the tool’s input_schema from the Pydantic model with CarrierInvoice.model_json_schema(), so the contract has one source.

The catch is in the output. Pydantic emits anyOf with a null branch for Optional fields. It includes title and default keys. It uses $defs references for nested models.

Does the API accept or transform each of these, especially under strict? That’s a question for the docs. The SDK offers helpers that prepare a schema for strict use; check the docs for their names in your SDK version.

Review the generated schema before shipping it, and keep a test that diffs it against a checked-in copy.
e568fe66d3:
Look at the message in the second branch. It states the numbers, names the field, and offers the two most likely causes. That’s what “specific validation error” means in 4.4. Section 13 explains why the wording matters more than any other part of the retry loop.

Now look at the first branch. It creates an issue with the code absent_source, a different class from semantic, because the correct response to it isn’t a retry. The loop reads the code to decide.
d25cfa4568:
A Spring service typically has a JSON Schema validator, a typed record, and one method per layer.

The sketch below uses Jackson for parsing, and the networknt json-schema-validator library for layer 1. Package names and method signatures vary by version, so check the docs for the version you pin. Layers 2 and 3 are plain code.

The model call hides behind a small interface, so the example doesn’t depend on an SDK signature. The adapter that wraps the Anthropic Java SDK or a WebClient call is a few lines. Write it against the SDK documentation.
2d732daff1:
In a Spring Boot application, make the validator a singleton bean created once from the tool schema. The schema then gets parsed at startup, not per request.

Bean Validation annotations on a record (@NotNull, @Pattern, @DecimalMin) can replace the Pydantic layer. A custom ConstraintValidator can hold the cross-field rule.

Spring AI also ships structured-output helpers that generate a schema from a Java type. Whether they fit a given Claude integration is a question for its documentation. The exam doesn’t test it.
7f14827de0:
When validation fails, the cheapest recovery is often another call. The 4.4 statement is specific about what makes that call effective. Send the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error.

Each of the three does work.

  • The original document lets the model re-read the source instead of reasoning from its memory of it.
  • The failed extraction shows exactly which answer was wrong. The model can change that and keep the parts that were right.
  • The specific error tells it what to look for.

Remove any one, and the retry degrades. Without the document, the model is guessing. Without the failed output, it may regenerate other mistakes. Without the error, it’s just the same call again.
edbb504d84:
Sampling is stochastic, so a bare retry occasionally succeeds by luck. But for the errors that matter most, the model’s mistake is systematic. It read the page one way. Given the same page and the same prompt, it’ll tend to read it the same way again.

A retry with no new information is a second sample from nearly the same distribution. Specific feedback changes the conditional distribution. Tell the model its line items sum to 3750.00 against a printed 3912.45, and “a missing line” becomes the most probable explanation. So it looks.

Companion example 07_retry_specific_vs_generic.py runs three fixable documents with each feedback style:
e76ba9a565:
The simulated model is built to repair what it’s told about and repeat what it isn’t. So the example demonstrates the harness: specific issues reach the model, and generic text carries nothing. It can’t prove how a real model behaves.

That specific feedback beats generic feedback is the documented guidance, and it matches wide practical experience. How big the effect is on your documents is something you measure. Run your own evaluation set with each feedback style (section 18).

Be sceptical of any pipeline whose authors can’t show that number.
027931ec7a:
The model’s previous turn ended in a tool_use block. So the next user message must open with a tool_result for that id (chapter 01’s pairing rule).

The natural place for the validation error is inside that result, marked is_error: true. That tells the model the call failed, and invites it to correct and call again. Companion example 15_retry_message_shape.py shows the wrong shape and the right one:
b121ed316d:
The conversation now holds the document, the failed call and the error, in the order the model needs to read them. In forced-tool mode, every turn is a tool call, and the turn after the error will be one too.

The auto-mode fallback from section 05 adds one more case. If the response had no tool call, there’s nothing to answer with a tool_result. So you append the assistant text and a plain user message telling the model to call the tool.
5277f4364d:
That function shows five design decisions, and each one is also an exam answer.

  • (1) The retry budget is a parameter. The loop exits through a review queue, never through an exception or an unbounded while.
  • (2) Each retry appends rather than restarts. The failed turn and the error stay in context, so the model sees what it did.
  • (3) The feedback is built from the issues, so the model reads the field path and the observed and expected values.
  • (4) The feedback includes the escape clause: “if a value is not printed, use null; do not invent or adjust”. Without it, pressure to satisfy a validator can produce a fabricated value (section 14).
  • (5) The loop returns the last record with a reason on failure, so a reviewer sees what the model produced and why it was rejected.
845c0fef46:
In production, two more things belong around this.

First, wrap the whole method in a timeout and a per-document cost cap. A retry doubles the token cost of a call, because the document and the failed turn are both resent.

Second, log every attempt with its issue codes. The sequence of codes per document is the most useful dataset you’ll have for improving the prompt, the schema and the validators.
c44cf91b3d:
A retry can only improve a result if the correct answer is reachable from the inputs. The exam guide states the converse plainly: retries are ineffective when the required information is absent from the source document.

Think of an invoice whose scan cuts off before the totals. An order form with no PO field. A contract that never states the renewal date. No amount of feedback creates a fact that isn’t on the page.

What retries do create, under pressure from a validator, is a plausible fabrication.
2d992d3687: Companion example 08_retry_cannot_help.py runs the scan with the amounts cut off. In variant A, the pipeline treats a null total as a validation failure and retries. In variant B, it recognises the null as legitimate and stops. Then a grounding check asks whether each extracted amount actually appears in the document:
47f8fc01d6:
Variant A is the dangerous result. Its status is ok. The record validates at every layer, the sum matches the total, and both numbers are made up. The pipeline reported success on a fabricated invoice, and spent an extra call to produce it.

Variant B costs one call. It returns the honest null with the model’s own note explaining it, and routes the record to review.

One decision in the harness separated A from B: is this a failure a retry can fix?
1ccb57ac87:
The loop can’t read the document the way a person does, so it needs evidence. Four sources are available, from cheapest to most expensive.

  • (1) A designed signal from the model. The nullable field plus notes gives the model a legitimate way to say “not printed”. A null with an explanatory note, on a field the validator wanted, is evidence of absence.
  • (2) A cheap deterministic check on the source text, like the regex in semantic_issues that looks for “total”, “amount due” or “balance due”.
  • (3) The pattern of failure across attempts. If the same field fails twice with the same issue and the model’s output doesn’t change, stop.
  • (4) A grounding check after a successful validation. Every extracted value that should be copied from the document must occur in it.

That last check is the backstop for the failure in variant A.
a77f07f843:
Grounding by string match is crude. It’ll raise false alarms on documents that print “1,200.5” or spell amounts out in words. Treat a grounding failure as a reason to review, not as proof of fabrication. It’s still valuable, because it turns an invisible failure into a visible one.

The same idea, applied to text fields, is a quote requirement. Ask the model for a short verbatim quote from the document next to each extracted value. Then check that the quote occurs in the source. Chapter 16 develops provenance and uses exactly this device.
b17ed3bf74: Route to review with context. The reviewer gets the document, the best record, the issues, the number of attempts and the model’s notes. Chapter 16 covers how to build the review queue, and how to calibrate which cases go there.
748be11a9a: Ask for a better source. For a truncated scan, the useful action is “request the missing page”. That’s a business process, not a model call. Include the reason code (absent_source) so the automation can trigger it.
1c1326f107: Look elsewhere. If the fact lives in another system (a PO in the ERP, matched by vendor and circuit), a lookup tool can supply it. That’s a different design, extraction plus enrichment, and the provenance should record the enrichment source.
5cb2b59f11:
A scenario where validation fails again and again on one field, with the same error each time, and asks what to do, is usually testing this.

Look for the signal that the information isn’t in the source: a null that’s correct, a scan with missing pages, a field the document type never carries.

The right answers stop retrying, record the null or the reason, and route to a person. The wrong answers raise the retry limit, rephrase the prompt, make the field required, or switch to a larger model. None of those can produce data that isn’t there.
d717c39bb1:
Everything so far concerns records that are wrong because the model misread a document.

A second kind of structured output fails differently. These are findings: things the model noticed, such as a code reviewer’s comments or a fraud screen’s alerts. Their error is the false positive, a finding that’s well-formed, plausible, and not worth acting on.

Chapter 11 covers how explicit criteria and few-shot examples reduce false positives. This section covers how to measure them. You can’t tune what you can’t slice.
f997a9ff09:
The exam’s device is a detected_pattern field on every finding. It’s a short snake_case name for the construct or rule that triggered the finding, chosen from a list in the prompt (null_deref_unchecked, sql_string_concat, local_var_naming, missing_javadoc).

When a developer dismisses a finding, record the dismissal against its pattern. You can then compute a false-positive rate per pattern. That’s the number that tells you where to act.
8fe1297d0b:
The overall dismissal rate of 58% invites a vague response: “make the reviewer more conservative”. Chapter 11 explains why that doesn’t work.

Per pattern, the picture changes. Two patterns produce nearly all the noise, and the one security pattern is clean. That points to a precise action: tighten or temporarily disable the two noisy patterns, and keep the others.

The per-pattern view also supports the trust argument from chapter 11. A category with a high false-positive rate teaches developers to ignore the whole tool. Removing it improves acceptance of the categories that matter.
f371af4122:
Three practical notes.

First, constrain the vocabulary. If detected_pattern is free text, the model will write “possible null pointer”, “null deref” and “NPE risk” for the same thing, and your groups fragment. Give a closed list in the prompt (with an "other" entry and a detail, as in section 09), or normalise after the fact.

Second, do not use the field to hide recall loss. Disabling a high-noise pattern is a deliberate trade. Log it, and re-evaluate when the criteria improve.

Third, the same device works outside code review. Tag extraction anomalies (currency_mismatch, date_out_of_period) and count which ones reviewers override. You’ll learn which of your validation rules is too strict.
29d5ff74b2:
A retry isn’t free. A design that treats it as free gets expensive at volume.

Each retry resends the document, the tool definition, the failed turn and the error. Its input is roughly double the first call’s, and its output is a full new tool call.

Run the numbers on the corpus in the companion folder. Companion example 14_pipeline_routing_report.py runs eight documents through the full pipeline:
692c70b3a8:
Read three things from it.

The first-pass rate (3/8) tells you how good your prompt and schema are. Retries lifted the final rate to 6/8, at the price of 5 extra calls: 13 calls for 8 documents, or 1.6 per document.

The two failures are different kinds, and their costs differ a lot. The absent-source case stopped after one call. The stubborn case burned three.

And a record that needed no retry isn’t the same as a record that’s correct. That’s why the first-pass number should be paired with a sampled human check (chapter 16).

If your first-pass rate is low, don’t lean on retries to cover for it. Fix the schema, the descriptions and the examples first. Every retry you avoid saves a full call.
8224cd4561:
Chapter 13 covers the Message Batches API in detail. Here are the facts that bear on this chapter.

  • Batches give a 50% discount on token costs. In exchange, processing is asynchronous, with a window of up to 24 hours and no latency guarantee.
  • Each request in a batch carries a custom_id you choose. Results come back keyed by that id, in no guaranteed order.
  • A single batch request is a single model call. The batch API doesn’t run a multi-turn tool conversation inside one request.
  • The docs also list structured outputs as supported in batch processing (check the docs for the details).
f8805f372c:
So for a retry loop, the loop moves out of the request and into your pipeline. You can’t have the batch call the model, validate, and call again inside one request.

Instead, you run the first pass as a batch. When it ends, you validate every result in your own code. Then you build a second batch containing only the failed custom_ids.

Each request in the second batch is a complete messages array: the original document, the assistant turn with the failed tool call, and a user turn with the tool_result (is_error) holding the specific feedback. To the API, that’s an ordinary single call that happens to have history.

Keep a retry round counter keyed by custom_id, so the budget survives across batches. Send the ones that exhaust it, or that carry absent_source, to review instead of into another batch.
32ae758efd:
When is batch the right place for extraction at all? When nobody is waiting for the answer: month-end invoice runs, back-fill of historic contracts, overnight classification. The 24-hour window and unordered results are a poor fit for a customer on a call.

Chapter 13 sets out the decision rules and the pitfalls (partial failures, expiry, result handling). The point to carry from this chapter: the validation and retry policy is identical. Only the transport changes.
1077b9fd4d:
A validated record isn’t a verified record. Validators catch inconsistency, not error. If the model misreads an amount the same way in both the line item and the printed total, no cross-check fires.

A layer above this chapter handles the remaining risk, and the exam tests it in Domain 5 (task statement 5.5). Three ideas from chapter 16 connect directly to what you’ve built here.
3d8af6c723: Field-level confidence, calibrated. You can add a confidence value per field and route low-confidence fields to review. The exam raises two cautions. A model’s self-reported confidence isn’t automatically calibrated, so compare it with labelled outcomes before you set a threshold on it. And aggregate accuracy hides weak segments, so measure by document type and field.
48bc4b84c0: Provenance. Store where each value came from: a short verbatim quote and a location. It makes review fast, because the reviewer sees the evidence. It enables the grounding check in section 14. And it’s the structure that multi-source synthesis needs. The citations feature is documented as incompatible with output_config.format (section 06), so a source_quote string in your own schema is the portable route.
3eac9976fd:
This chapter hands off to that layer. The validators and the retry loop remove the errors you can detect by rule and recover by re-reading.

What’s left goes to people, with the evidence attached: the record, the issue codes, the notes, the attempt count, the quotes. If your needs_review result carries those, the review queue in chapter 16 can be built on it without changing the extraction code.
8082d530a5:
A structured-output pipeline has two things to test, and they need different methods.

The harness is the code around the model. It’s deterministic, and you can test it exhaustively offline with a scripted fake. Does it send the contract it should? Does it bound its retries and stop on an absent source? Does it put the issue in the right message, and route each failure to the right place?

The model’s behaviour on your documents is statistical. The only honest test is a labelled evaluation set run against the live model.

Don’t confuse the two. A passing offline test suite tells you nothing about extraction accuracy. And a good live accuracy figure won’t protect you from a retry-loop bug that only fires on a rare path.
a5c6e9fc27:
Each test pins a behaviour the exam also asks about.

The one most worth copying into your own suite is the last. It asserts that a record which passes the schema can still be rejected. A future refactor that “simplifies” validation to schema-only would make that test fail. That’s exactly its purpose.

Add tests for your normalisation rules (the parenthesised credit from section 10), for every issue code, and for the auto-mode fallback that treats prose as a failed attempt.
8eb6310d82: Build a set of real documents, a few dozen to start, each with the correct record written by a person. Run the live pipeline and compute these figures, per document type and per field where you can:
25feb38057:
Use the evaluation set as a gate, the same way chapters 05 and 11 use theirs. Any change to the schema, descriptions, examples, validators or model must not reduce the accuracy figures, or increase fabrication-after-retry, on the held-out set.

Companion example 17_live_optional.py runs the pipeline against the real API when a key is present. The author of this guide hasn’t run it live. Treat it as a starting point, and check it against the current SDK documentation.
df29894f49:
Case C deserves a final word, because it looks like diligence. “Repair” sounds responsible: the validator found a discrepancy, so reconcile it. But which side is wrong?

If the model dropped a line, the printed total is right, and your repair overwrote the truth with the model’s error. If the printed total is a previous balance, the line items are right, and the repair may break those too.

You can’t tell from the numbers alone. That’s exactly why the record keeps both, and why a person or a specific retry decides.
0488516868: The questions for 4.3 and 4.4 are written around a pipeline that works most of the time and fails in one specific way. Identify the failure class first: syntax, schema, semantic, or absent information. Then pick the mechanism that addresses that class and nothing else.
1792238225:
The cause is the schema. A required non-null field leaves the model no honest way to report absence, so it invents.

B removes the pressure and states the rule in the description. A detects the symptom after the fact and sends the record to review. That’s useful as a second layer, but it leaves the cause in place. C retries a case where the information is absent, and a retry is more likely to produce another invented value. D treats a design problem as a capability problem.
9b8c909e03:
This is a semantic error, and schemas can’t detect those.

B exposes the disagreement in the record, verifies it independently in code, and uses the specific discrepancy for one retry. A bounds individual values and can’t relate two fields. C gives the model a goal it can meet by altering a number.

D discards the printed total. But that total is the only way to notice a missed line item. A dropped surcharge would now produce a confidently wrong total.
081f40ac74:
Retries can’t supply information that isn’t in the source. The repeated identical failure and the reviewers’ finding are the signals.

C stops spending calls, keeps the honest null and the reason, and sends the case where the fix actually lives: a better source. A and D spend more on the same impossible task. B is the fabrication trap from scenario 1. It makes the model produce a number that doesn’t exist.
56afe4b623:
any guarantees a structured call while leaving the choice of schema to the model. That’s the requirement.

auto allows a prose reply, which would break the contract that every message returns a record. Forcing the invoice tool makes the model squeeze credit notes and POs into the wrong schema. none disables the very mechanism that gives structure.

In production, add an unclear or other path, for example a fourth tool for “unrecognised document”. any has no way to say none of these fit. And check whether your model supports any at all, since some current models reject it (section 05).
e663506b76:
The goal is diagnosis. detected_pattern turns dismissals into per-pattern false-positive rates. Those show whether two patterns cause most of the noise.

A relies on a self-reported confidence that hasn’t been calibrated, so the 0.8 cut is arbitrary (chapter 16). C is the vague instruction that chapter 11 shows doesn’t change what the model reports. D adds cost and a second model with the same blind spots, and it still doesn’t tell the team which categories are noisy.

After B, the fixes are chapter 11’s: sharpen the criteria, add examples, or temporarily disable the worst patterns.
479aab274b: Use the companion folder ccarf-companion/12-structured-output-retry/. Everything runs offline. Create a virtual environment with pip install anthropic jsonschema pydantic. The examples import the Anthropic types for the fake client.
1a7736705e: In extraction_lib.py, change the PO-number description from “null if no PO is printed. Never infer.” to “PO number”. Does the simulation change? Explain why not, and what that says about what the simulation can and can’t test.
d59f4ce509: Edit feedback_text so it leaves out the escape clause (“if a value is not printed, use null”). Re-run 08_retry_cannot_help.py with stop_on_absent=False and compare with the original. Write down which hypothesis from the README the example encodes.
cec25b340b: Add a new document to DOCS: a credit memo that prints a negative total in parentheses. Make a pipeline test fail before you teach the semantic check about parentheses. Then fix it.
a69d2c58ee: Run 18_forced_choice_rejected_models.py. Change the fake so the first auto-mode attempt returns prose on every document, and a tool call only after the nudge. What happens to the attempt counts in 14?
f1ae6037b8:
Done when: you can explain, without notes:

  • why a schema-valid record can be wrong;
  • why a required non-null field produces invented values;
  • why a retry on an absent field fabricates;
  • what each of the four tool_choice settings does, and when a model may reject two of them;
  • what a specific feedback message contains.

You should also have a test that fails if someone changes the pipeline to accept schema-valid records without semantic checks.
